title: Parades and marching bands as influences
summary: Hug says marching bands and drum beats inspired him as much as pianists; pianists who had left; New Orleans vs Dixieland term.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: Would you say that your, the important influences, the piano style, the piano playing that influenced you came from that area more than any other? From the parades?

John, this is something now, you asked me a very good question. I like that question because that's very good. I can say that even though my basic love was piano, no. These piano players, even though they were beautiful, it was not the only thing that influenced me. Just a drum beat coming down the street was a great inspiration. Just to hear that beat. I see. Or just to hear a two or three or four piece band playing somewhere. Or to hear a bunch of guys get together that could hardly play. But at least they had the feeling, the spirit, you know. I mean, all of these things, I mean, they had a great influence on me.
And most piano players, I take it around that time, let's say, set in 1915 or 1910 or whatever. You were born in 1910. We're band pianists.

They weren't so pianists. Band pianists, right. And you see, a lot of the good pianists that had kind of left around here by the time that I was coming up. Jelly Roll had been, Jelly Roll was gone. Clarence Williams was gone. Clarence Williams was gone. Clarence Williams was gone. Tony Jackson was gone. You had many, many, I guess, were still around here. You had many local fellows, local pianists around town. Steve Lewis was around here, which was an excellent, excellent black pianist. Wonderful. And, well, like I say, the pianist, I always, I always loved the pianist. You know, anywhere there was a piano player, that was, that was my, my, my ideal right there. But really, I got inspiration from, from many of the marching bands. Just listening to, listening to them play, play that feudal music, and, and, and happy marching music, you know. The marching music, I think, is so inspirational. If this doesn't inspire you, well, you just don't have music in you, that's all. It inspires you to do greater things, let me put it that way. It inspired me.
Did they, did the marching bands play Dixieland? Was that a term?
They always played two beat, don't you think, Chad?

We say, we, we use the term two beat, but, well, not two beat, uh, just, March music, which was traditional. New Orleans March music. New Orleans March music, which is, Monk, Monk Hazel used to always tell me, he used to always say, oh man, I hate to, hate to hear him use the word Dixieland,

and, and type you with, with just Dixieland, because he says, really, it's New Orleans music, you know. Of course, Dixieland, we know it's, it's part of this, part of this scene too.
